report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: obtained under factorial manipulations of information quality.
These analysis are conventionally restricted to correct responses, leaving unclear whether condition-dependent errors can distort the architecture-diagnostic survivor interaction contrast (SIC).
We used diffusion-model simulations to examine whether SIC-based diagnoses remain valid when errors differ in prevalence and timing across the high-high, high-low, low-high, and low-low conditions.
We first implemented coactive processing using the partitioned circular diffusion model under AND and OR task rules.
Cross-trial variability in drift magnitude produced slow errors, whereas variability in the decision boundary produced fast errors.

Although the expected stochastic ordering of the correct-response survivor functions was generally preserved, both mechanisms progressively attenuated the characteristic negative-then-positive coactive SIC, causing it to resemble the entirely positive signature of parallel self-terminating processing.
We then generalized the analysis to a parallel self-terminating architecture implemented using linear-drift, linear-infinitesimal-variance model.
Racing generated slow errors even without cross-trial drift-rate variability, but the expected positive SIC remained robust while the error pattern was relatively similar across factorial conditions.
Adding drift-rate variability differentiated the condition-specific error patterns and progressively weakened the SIC.

These findings show that presence of errors compromises architectural diagnosis when their timing and prevalence differ across four factorial conditions, causing correct-response selection to reshape the contributing RT distributions unequally.
Conditional accuracy functions provide a practical companion measure for identifying this risk.

Systems Factorial Technology (SFT; Townsend & Nozawa, 1995; Little et al., 2017) was developed as a non-parametric framework for inferring the properties of an informationprocessing system directly from response-time (RT) distributions.
text.formatted: Systems Factorial Technology (SFT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Townsend & Nozawa, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Little et al., 2017)</ref> was developed as a non-parametric framework for inferring the properties of an informationprocessing system directly from response-time (RT) distributions.

text.text: Rather than specifying a particular generative mechanism, SFT derives diagnostic predictions from factorial manipulations of experimental conditions and distribution-level contrasts, including the mean interaction contrast (MIC), survivor interaction contrast (SIC), and capacity coefficient (C(t)).
These measures provide converging evidence about processing architecture, stopping rules, and workload capacity.

Because SFT does not require researchers to assume a particular distribution of observed outcomes or a specific response-generating process, it is well suited for distinguishing between theories that share similar parametric implementations or produce overlapping observable patterns in conventional analysis (Townsend, 1971; Khodadadi & Townsend, 2015; Wilken & Ma, 2004).

text.text: Its relatively minimal assumptions have supported applications across a broad range of domains, including visual search (Fifić et al., 2008), categorization (Blunden et al., 2015; Fifić & Townsend, 2010; Little et al., 2011 Little et al., , 2013;; Moneer et al., 2016), face perception (Cheng et al., 2018; Fifić & Townsend, 2010; Cheng & Little, 2025), numerical processing (Garrett et al., 2019), and memory-based change detection (Blunden et al., 2022; Fong et al., 2024).

text.text: Empirical application of SFT is commonly based on the double factorial paradigm (DFP).

In this design, the quality of two information sources is manipulated independently at high and low levels, producing four factorial conditions: high-high (HH), high-low (HL), lowhigh (LH), and low-low (LL).
Under the assumption of selective influence, manipulating the quality of one source changes the processing of that source without directly changing the processing of the other.
Lower information quality is expected to slow processing, producing an ordered relationship among the RT distributions across four factorial conditions.
The HH condition is generally associated with the fastest responses, the LL condition with the slowest responses, and the two mixed conditions with intermediate response times.
This stochastic ordering provides the basis for combining the four survivor functions into the SIC.

Different processing architectures and stopping rules predict distinct SIC shapes, allowing combinations of architecture and stopping rule to be distinguished without specifying a detailed parametric model of the underlying decision process.
These diagnostic predictions are derived from the completion-time survivor functions generated by four factorial manipulations.
In empirical applications, however, the relevant survivors are generally constructed from correct-response RTs.

SFT studies therefore often seek to limit error rates by using relatively easy or highly discriminable stimuli, training and repeatedly testing a small number of observers across multiple sessions (Fifić et al., 2008; Fox & Houpt, 2016), or calibrating stimulus salience levels to each observer's performance (Glvan et al., 2019).

Recent studies have extended SFT to incorporate error responses through several approaches (Little et al., 2022; Gondan & Legner, 2026), including modifications of workload-capacity measures (Eidels et al., 2010) and assessment functions that jointly characterize response time and accuracy (Townsend & Altieri, 2012).

text.text: Nevertheless, the consequences of excluding errors from analysis, at a theoretical level, remain insufficiently understood.
This question is important because the same factorial manipulation used to generate RT differences will likely also generate differences in response accuracy.
Lower-quality information is not only processed more slowly but is also more likely to produce an incorrect response.
Consequently, the four DFP conditions may differ in both their RT distributions and their error rates, with errors typically occurring more frequently in the lower-quality conditions.
This is not an exceptional feature of the task or evidence of a failed manipulation; rather, it is a natural consequence of varying the quality of the information available to the observer.

Maintaining high overall accuracy can reduce the magnitude of these differences, but it does not resolve the theoretical question of whether the excluded error responses contain part of the effect produced by the factorial manipulation.
The present study therefore aims to determine whether SIC-based diagnoses of processing architecture remain valid when the DFP produces substantial errors.

Specifically, we examine whether differences in error rates across the HH, HL, LH, and LL conditions alter the correct-response RT distributions and whether excluding these errors distorts the SIC despite the underlying processing architecture remaining unchanged.

text.text: In this model, evidence accumulation is described as a diffusion process (or equivalently, Wiener process) that evolves over time toward one of two decision boundaries.

The drift rate specifies the average rate at which evidence accumulates toward a boundary, the starting point specifies the initial position of the accumulation process relative to two boundaries, and the boundary separation specifies the total amount of evidence required before a response is executed. text.text: In the diffusion model literature, fast and slow errors arise from distinct sources of variability that operate across trials.

Variability in starting point, which reflects trial-to-trial fluctuations in pre-decisional bias toward one response alternative, increases the probability of rapid boundary crossings at the incorrect boundary and therefore produces fast errors.

Similarly, variability in boundary separation, which reflects trial-to-trial changes in the amount of evidence required before responding, can also contribute to relatively fast errors when the effective boundary is reduced on some trials.

Variability in drift rate, which reflects fluctuations in the quality or strength of evidence extracted from the stimulus, leads to slow errors because incorrect responses tend to arise on trials with weak or misleading evidence, resulting in longer accumulation times before reaching the incorrect boundary.

The inclusion of cross-trial parameter variability provides a systematic account of how different sources of variability generate distinct temporal patterns of errors at the level of response time distributions, thereby allowing sequential sampling models to accommodate a wide range of behavioral patterns.

However, the same assumption of cross-trial parameter variability has also been challenged for introducing excessive model flexibility (Jones & Dzhafarov, 2014; but see Smith et al., 2014 and Heathcote et al., 2014 for further discussions). text.text: The presence of cross-trial parameter variability is especially meaningful for current study, as they may influence the SFT double factorial conditions to different degrees.

For example, variability in evidence quality may exert a greater influence when mean evidence strength is low, producing more pronounced changes in the RT and accuracy distributions of the LL and mixed conditions than in the HH condition.

Because distribution-level contrasts such as the SIC depend on specific relationships among all four factorial conditions, any source of variability that reshapes these distributions non-uniformly may change the observed architectural signature.

The present study uses simulations to investigate whether an SIC calculated from correct-response RTs remains diagnostic in the presence of errors and, specifically, to disentangle the effects of slow and fast errors.

We hold processing architecture constant while introducing the same degree of parameter variability across the HH, HL, LH, and LL conditions, allowing the resulting error rates and error-time relationships to differ naturally with stimulus quality.

We then examine whether excluding these errors reshapes the four correct-response distributions sufficiently to alter the SIC, and whether this effect depends on errors being concentrated among relatively slow or fast responses.

Our results show that SIC distortion emerges primarily when the prevalence and timing of errors differ across factorial conditions, resulting in unequal selection of the correct-response distributions.
Under these circumstances, the SIC can become substantially attenuated and may resemble the prediction of a different architecture, even when stochastic ordering remains intact.

Systems Factorial Technology (SFT) is a meta-theoretical framework designed to diagnose the structure of multiple-source information processing (Townsend et al., 2018; Townsend & Nozawa, 1995).
text.formatted: Systems Factorial Technology (SFT) is a meta-theoretical framework designed to diagnose the structure of multiple-source information processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Townsend et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Townsend & Nozawa, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: SFT seeks to draw qualitative inferences about how multiple sources of information are combined to guide a single response.
A central advantage of SFT is that its inferences are non-parametric and model-free.
That is, SFT does not assume a particular distributional form for RTs, nor does it rely on parameter estimation within a specified generative model.

Instead, conclusions about processing structure are derived directly from order relationships and contrasts among empirical RT distributions obtained from carefully constrained experimental conditions.
SFT characterizes a processing system based on three primary properties: architecture, stopping rule, and workload capacity.
Architecture refers to how multiple sources of information are temporally and functionally organized during processing.
SFT distinguishes three processing architectures: serial, parallel, and coactive.
In a serial architecture, sources are processed one at a time following a sequence.
The order of processing may be fixed or flexible across trials, and whether processing proceeds to subsequent sources depends on the stopping rule, which is introduced in the next paragraph.
In a parallel architecture, multiple sources are processed simultaneously in separate channels.
Processing across channels may be independent or may involve interactions that produce facilitatory or inhibitory effects (Eidels et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Processing across channels may be independent or may involve interactions that produce facilitatory or inhibitory effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Eidels et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Despite such interactions, information remains distributed across distinct processing channels.
In a coactive architecture, multiple sources are processed simultaneously but pooled into a single processing stream.
Rather than being processed in separate channels, information from all sources jointly contributes to a unified decision process (Houpt & Townsend, 2011; Townsend & Houpt, 2025).
text.formatted: Rather than being processed in separate channels, information from all sources jointly contributes to a unified decision process <ref type="bibr">(Houpt & Townsend, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Townsend & Houpt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The stopping rule specifies the condition under which processing terminates.
SFT distinguishes between self-terminating and exhaustive stopping rules.
Under a self-terminating stopping rule, processing ends as soon as sufficient information is obtained to support a response, and the remaining sources need not complete processing.
Under an exhaustive stopping rule, processing exhausts all sources, regardless of whether sufficient information for a response has been obtained earlier.
Stopping rules are conceptually independent of architecture, and different combinations of architecture and stopping rule yield distinct predictions for processing time.

For example, a serial exhaustive system predicts that total processing time equals the sum of processing times across all sequentially processed sources, whereas a parallel self-terminating system predicts that total processing time corresponds to the minimum processing time among the sources sufficient to trigger a response.
Workload capacity describes how efficiently a processing system handles increases in processing load, such as the addition of information source that requires processing.
SFT distinguishes among three capacity regimes.
A system exhibits unlimited capacity when processing efficiency remains unchanged as workload increases, indicating that additional sources do not impair performance.
A system exhibits limited capacity when processing efficiency decreases with increasing workload, consistent with constraints on total processing resources or inhibitory interactions among sources.
A system exhibits super capacity when processing efficiency increases with workload, potentially suggesting facilitative interactions among sources.

SFT identifies above three properties commonly through the Double Factorial Paradigm (DFP), an experimental framework specifically designed to isolate properties of information processing structure through selective manipulation of multiple (typically two) information sources.

In typical DFP experiments, an observer is presented with either two stimuli that occupy distinct locations (Fifić et al., 2008; Fifić et al., 2010) or a single stimulus that comprises two physically distinct features (Fifić et al., 2010; Little et al., 2011; Little et al., 2013; Moneer et al., 2016; Little & Moneer, 2026).

text.text: The observer's task is to make a single response based on the joint status of these two sources.
Two task variants are most commonly used.
In an OR task, the observer responds affirmatively if either of two sources is present, whereas in an AND task, an affirmative response requires both sources to be present.
Importantly, two tasks naturally impose different optimal stopping rules (Fifić et al., 2008).

text.text: In an AND task, correct responses require exhaustive processing of all sources, whereas in an OR task, processing can self-terminate as soon as a target is identified, yielding correct responses with reduced processing demands.
Although nonoptimal stopping rules are possible, their use may lead to reduced accuracy or increased response times (Little et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although nonoptimal stopping rules are possible, their use may lead to reduced accuracy or increased response times <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Little et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Within each task, the quality or salience of each source is manipulated independently, typically at two levels (e.g., high vs. low salience).
Salience is irrelevant to the response itself-both high and low salience targets are treated as present-but it systematically influences the speed with which information is processed.

By independently varying the salience of each source, the DFP creates a full factorial set of conditions that selectively influence processing time at each source without altering response instructions.
The inferential logic of the DFP depends on selective influence: each factorial manipulation must affect only the processing of its corresponding information source.
Increasing the salience of a source is also assumed to selectively accelerate its processing, producing an expected stochastic ordering among the observed RT distributions.
This ordering provides an observable check on the effects required by selective influence, although it does not by itself establish that the assumption holds.
When these requirements are satisfied, contrasts among the four RT distributions can be interpreted in terms of processing architecture, stopping rule, and workload capacity.
In current study, we focus on the inference for architecture and stopping rule by computing the survivor interaction contrast.

In the standard two-source DFP, the quality of each stimulus is independently varied between a high (H) and a low (L) level, yielding four experimental conditions (HH, HL, LH, LL).

The cardinal and polar representations are mathematically equivalent, while emphasizing different aspects of the accumulation dynamics.
The cardinal formulation highlights the contribution of each source dimension separately.

Changes in 𝜇 % and 𝜇 & can be directly interpreted as changes in the quality or strength of evidence associated with the corresponding source, making this representation particularly useful when stimulus manipulations are assumed to cause independent effects along each dimension.

text.text: Although the two components retain source-specific interpretations, they do not drive independent decision processes.
Instead, they jointly determine the evolution and termination of a single diffusion trajectory, so information from the two sources is pooled within a common decision process.
The polar formulation better emphasizes this joint properties of the accumulation process.

The magnitude ‖𝜇‖ primarily determines response speed by controlling how rapidly the diffusion process approaches the decision boundary, whereas the direction 𝜃 * governs which region of the boundary is most likely to be reached, shaping response choice probabilities.
Analogously, the 𝜂 rad and 𝜂 tan capture sources of cross-trial variability with distinct effects on the resulting distributions.
Increasing 𝜂 )+, increases cross-trial variability in ‖𝜇‖ while holding 𝜃 * constant, whereas increasing 𝜂 -+. increases cross-trial variability in 𝜃 * while holding ‖𝜇‖ constant.
Psychologically, when 𝜂 -+. = 0 , variability is confined to trial-to-trial fluctuations in the effective rate of evidence accumulation, assuming stable stimulus feature representation.
Conversely, when 𝜂 )+, = 0, variability is confined to fluctuations in the balance of evidence across stimulus dimensions, while the overall rate of accumulation remains constant.
In later simulations, we show that this distinction has important implications for the robustness of SFT diagnostics.
The decision boundary parameter, 𝑎, specifies the radius of the circular absorbing boundary and therefore the amount of accumulated evidence required to terminate the decision process.
In later simulations, we assume the boundary varies across trials according to a uniform distribution.

A smaller value of 𝑎 places the boundary closer to the starting point, producing shorter RTs but increasing the probability that moment-to-moment noise drives the process into an incorrect response region.
A larger value requires the process to travel farther before termination, generally producing longer but more accurate responses.
Psychologically, cross-trial variability in 𝑎 represents fluctuations in response caution, such that the amount of evidence required before responding varies across trials.
This variability produces a mixture of relatively fast, error-prone decisions arising from lower boundaries and slower, more accurate decisions arising from higher boundaries.
As with standard diffusion models, pCDM also includes parameters governing withintrial diffusion noise and non-decision time.
The within-trial diffusion noise governs momentto-moment stochasticity in the accumulation process, and non-decision time captures peripheral processes such as stimulus encoding and motor execution.
In the present work, these two parameters are held constant across all simulations.

This design choice ensures that any observed changes in RT distributions, response accuracy, or SFT diagnostics can be attributed to differences in drift structure, decision boundary, or their respective cross-trial variability.

The structure of pCDM places it conceptually close to several influential models of multidimensional decision making that combine probabilistic continuous evidence representations with stochastic decision processes (Ashby, 2000; Nosofsky & Stanton, 2005; Fifić et al., 2010; Blunden et al., 2022).

text.text: One particularly relevant example is the stochastic General Recognition Theory (sGRT) model (Ashby, 2000).
text.formatted: One particularly relevant example is the stochastic General Recognition Theory (sGRT) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashby, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As discussed below, although the pCDM and sGRT differ in their formal assumptions and intended applications, they share important structural features and therefore provide useful points of comparison.

The sGRT extends the classic General Recognition Theory (Ashby & Townsend, 1986) by introducing moment-to-moment fluctuation in stimulus representation, which in turn drive a decision process modelled using a one-dimensional Wiener process.
text.formatted: The sGRT extends the classic General Recognition Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ashby & Townsend, 1986)</ref> by introducing moment-to-moment fluctuation in stimulus representation, which in turn drive a decision process modelled using a one-dimensional Wiener process.

text.text: In sGRT, perceptual processing is described within a multidimensional stimulus space, where the momentary outputs of perceptual channels evolve stochastically over time.

At each moment, channel outputs are combined through a linear discriminant function to compute a scalar discriminant value, which then drives a univariate diffusion process with two absorbing barriers that predicts accuracy and response time.

In this way, sGRT implements a two-stage coactive architecture, in which perceptual representation and evidence accumulation are formally distinct but theoretically linked through the discriminant function (Ashby 2000, Figure 3).
text.formatted: In this way, sGRT implements a two-stage coactive architecture, in which perceptual representation and evidence accumulation are formally distinct but theoretically linked through the discriminant function <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashby 2000</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>).

text.text: The pCDM and sGRT represent two different ways of obtaining RT predictions from the classic GRT and share similar conceptual foundations.

In both models, probabilistic stimulus representations are modelled using bivariate normal distribution, and decision are made by setting boundaries that directly partition the stimulus representation space.
In this sense, both models preserve the core representational commitments of GRT while embedding them within stochastic decision dynamics.
The two models differ, however, in how stimulus representation and evidence accumulation are organized, and in the range of decision tasks they naturally accommodate.
In sGRT, stimulus representation unfolds in a multidimensional perceptual space, whereas evidence accumulation occurs in a separate, unidimensional space derived from that representation.
Decision boundaries operate in the representation space, generate scalar input for the accumulation stage.

By contrast, in pCDM the stimulus-related evidence space and the accumulation space are unified: evidence accumulates directly as a two-dimensional diffusion process toward a circular absorbing barriers defined in the same space.
Decision boundaries directly cut the absorbing barriers to generate RT and choice prediction.

As a consequence of these structural differences, sGRT applies most naturally to tasks involving binary classification judgements based on two-feature stimuli, while pCDM accommodates multialternative classification of such stimuli, including four-way identification as illustrated in Figure 2, and binary judgment by appropriately grouping the partitioned response regions, as we later demonstrate in simulation.

text.text: Before turning to formal simulations and diagnostics, it is helpful to discuss how the structure of pCDM bears on key concepts in SFT, particularly the notion of coactive processing.

At a conceptual level, SFT characterizes coactive processing as a system in which information from multiple sources is pooled into a single processing channel before a decision is made (Townsend & Nozawa, 1995).
text.formatted: At a conceptual level, SFT characterizes coactive processing as a system in which information from multiple sources is pooled into a single processing channel before a decision is made <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Townsend & Nozawa, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: The pooling could take various form, though the most welldeveloped schemes assume evidence strength from two source are directly summed to be compared against a single decision criterion (Schwarz, 1989; Schwarz, 1994; Houpt & Townsend, 2011; Townsend & Houpt, 2025).
text.formatted: The pooling could take various form, though the most welldeveloped schemes assume evidence strength from two source are directly summed to be compared against a single decision criterion <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Schwarz, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Schwarz, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Houpt & Townsend, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Townsend & Houpt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Compared with coactive simulations in much of the existing literature, pCDM exhibits several noteworthy properties.
First, pCDM combines information from multiple stimuli in a theoretically tighter manner.

Previous studies have often simulated coactive processing by summing drift rates from two independent one-dimensional diffusion or deterministic accumulating processes that terminate at a shared decision boundary.
While such formulations allow information from multiple sources to influence response time, they effectively reduce coactivation to additive contributions at the decision stage.

As a result, potential interactions between stimulus dimensions, and the consequential joint influence on response time and accuracy, are not explicitly represented within the accumulation process itself.

In contrast, pCDM implements coactivation at a more fundamental level by modeling evidence accumulation as a single two-dimensional diffusion process with jointly distributed drift rates, such that information from multiple sources jointly determines both the direction and speed of accumulation, which in turn generates joint prediction of RT and accuracy.
Second, pCDM provides a unified theoretical framework for comparing performance across different task instructions.

SFT has been applied primarily to OR tasks, AND tasks, and has recently been extended to full identification tasks, in which observers report the state of each stimulus by pressing uniquely labeled responses (Howard et al., 2021; Howard et al., 2026).
text.formatted: SFT has been applied primarily to OR tasks, AND tasks, and has recently been extended to full identification tasks, in which observers report the state of each stimulus by pressing uniquely labeled responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Howard et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Howard et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: SFT has developed distinct architectural and capacity predictions for each instruction type, treating them as analytically related but formally separate cases.
When these instruction types are applied to the same stimulus configuration, pCDM provides a theoretical account across all three tasks using a common set of diffusion parameters.
Differences in observed distributions arise not from changes in the accumulation process itself, but from differences in how decision outcomes are mapped onto responses.
Within pCDM, this mapping is implemented by partitioning boundary-hitting locations differently across decision bounds.
As a result, pCDM offers a unified process-level account in which task instructions modulate response categorization rather than the underlying evidence accumulation dynamics.

Finally, pCDM provides a principled way to examine SFT predictions in the presence of mixed data arising from multiple latent subprocesses, a situation that is likely to occur in empirical experiments but is difficult to disentangle directly from observed responses.

For example, consider an OR task trial in which both stimuli are present, the correct response may come from either correctly identifying stimuli at both locations or from only identifying a stimulus at a single location while failing to identify the other.
The latter case, while still generate correct response, includes incorrect stimulus identification.
Within pCDM, such mixtures arise naturally from the stochastic properties of the accumulation process.

Changes in tangential cross-trial drift-rate variability, 𝜂 tan , alter the relative proportions of diffusion trajectories terminating in different boundary regions, thereby changing the composition of latent subprocesses contributing to correct responses.

By explicitly monitoring simulated mixture proportions, pCDM enables systematic investigation of how such latent variability interacts with SFT diagnostics, without requiring empirical separation of subprocesses that are observationally indistinguishable.

Taken together, these properties illustrate how pCDM provides a coherent process-level framework for examining SFT predictions across task instructions, mixture structures, and sources of variability.

Decomposing cross-trial drift-rate variability into radial and tangential components reveals that these two sources of variability have dissociable empirical consequences.

Variability in drift direction leaves CAFs largely flat and preserves the characteristic coactive SIC pattern, while variability in drift magnitude produces declining CAFs, indicating the emergence of slow errors, and progressively attenuates the SIC.

text.text: In the OR task, observers respond affirmatively when at least one stimulus is present, and respond negatively only when both stimuli are absent.
Unlike the AND task, in which correct responses uniquely require correct identification of both stimuli, correct responses in the OR task can arise from multiple underlying outcomes.
When both stimuli are present, a correct response may result from correctly identifying both stimuli or from identifying the presence of only one stimulus while failing to identify the other.
Within pCDM, these outcomes correspond naturally to different boundary-hitting regions.

Correct OR responses are generated by diffusion trajectories terminating in the first, second, or fourth quadrants, corresponding respectively to identification of both stimuli, identification of stimulus 2 alone, or identification of stimulus 1 alone.
To obtain the RT distribution for correct OR responses, we aggregate the boundary-hitting times from all three quadrants into a single distribution.

Consequently, the correct RT distribution in the OR task depends not only on the timing of boundary crossings within each quadrant, but also on the relative proportions of trajectories terminating in each quadrant.

Whereas the AND-task RT distribution is determined solely by trajectories in the first quadrant, the OR-task RT distribution reflects both temporal properties of accumulation-primarily governed by ‖𝜇‖ and 𝜂 )+, -and changes in response composition, which are primarily governed by 𝜂 -+.
As in the AND task, we first map the effects of cross-trial drift rate variability onto CAFs to identify which form of variability produces slow errors.

These results demonstrate that an unchanged coactive architecture can produce qualitatively different SIC patterns once error responses are excluded.

In this section, we extend the analysis to a racing-diffusion implementation of parallel self-terminating processing, a benchmark system in SFT.

In racing diffusion models, each stimulus channel is modeled using two single-boundary diffusion processes, each represents an alternative stimulus-identification and races to determine the response and completion time.
With two stimuli, four diffusion processes evolve in parallel, and the system-level response and RT are determined according to the self-terminating stopping rule.

Alongside the standard style diffusion model (Ratcliff, 1978; Ratcliff et al., 2016; Smith & Ratcliff, 2022), racing diffusion models have also been extensively used in modeling discrete-outcome decision (Pike, 1966; Logan, 1996; Townsend & Ashby, 1983; Usher & McClelland, 2001; Smith & Van Zandt, 2000; Hawkins & Heathcote, 2021; Smith, 2023). Ratcliff (2018) extended the racing diffusion structure to a model of continuous-outcome decision, the spatially continuous diffusion model (SCDM, see also Fennell & Ratcliff, 2023). Smith et al. (2026) compared the CDM and SCDM on three perceptual experiments that showed quantitatively different patterns of RT and errors, and found both model structures provided good accounts of performance.

text.text: The LDLIV is a dual-diffusion model that was developed to embody three properties commonly associated with neural evidence representations: activation remains nonnegative, approaches saturation at high levels, and is represented separately for each response alternative.
These properties arise from the dynamics of the diffusion process itself rather than from an externally imposed reflecting boundary.
In addition, its moment-to-moment variability increases with its current activation state, capturing the general neural property that firing-rate variability tends to increase with mean activity.

Smith (2023) compared the LDLIV with the standard diffusion model and two alternative dual-diffusion models: a race between Wiener processes with lower reflecting boundaries and a race between unconstrained single-boundary Wiener processes.

Across benchmark numerosity-discrimination and spatial-cuing datasets, the LDLIV and standard diffusion model provided similarly successful accounts of choice probabilities and correct and error RT distributions, although the standard diffusion model was more parsimonious.
The LDLIV performed somewhat better for the numerosity data, whereas the standard diffusion model was favoured for the spatial-cuing data, particularly after penalizing model complexity.
Both models nevertheless performed appreciably better than the other racing-diffusion models.

In particular, the unconstrained racing model could generate slow errors without drift-rate variability but did not adequately reproduce their magnitude and distribution across the full range of empirical conditions.
These comparisons support the LDLIV as a tractable and neurally-motivated implementation of racing evidence accumulation.

To apply the LDLIV within the present parallel self-terminating simulation, we represented each stimulus by a pair of racing accumulators, one associated with the correct identification and the other with error.
We held the total medium drift rate (𝜇 456 ) constant within each pair and manipulated stimulus quality by varying the proportion (𝑝) allocated to the correct accumulator.
The medium drift rates for the correct and error accumulators were therefore given by 𝑝𝜇 456 and (1 -𝑝)𝜇 456 , respectively.

Under high-quality stimulation, most of the total drift was assigned to the correct accumulator (𝑝 = 0.9), whereas under low-quality stimulation the drift was divided more evenly between the correct and error accumulators (𝑝 = 0.55).
The HH, HL, LH, and LL conditions were generated by combining the corresponding high-and low-quality drift allocations across the two stimulus channels.

Racing competition can generate slow errors without compromising the SIC when its effects on the factorial conditions are sufficiently similar.

SIC attenuation emerges when added drift-rate variability produces increasingly condition-dependent relationships between accuracy and RT, causing error exclusion to reshape the four correct-response distributions unequally.
The relevant threat to architectural diagnosis is therefore not slow errors per se, but their differential influence on the distributions entering the SIC.
The present study examined whether SIC-based diagnoses remain robust when correctresponse RT distributions are selected from data containing temporally heterogeneous and condition-dependent errors.

Using the pCDM, we held a coactive architecture constant while generating slow errors through cross-trial variability in drift magnitude and fast errors through variability in the decision boundary, under both AND and OR task rules.

In each case, the expected stochastic ordering was generally preserved, yet increasingly differentiated CAFs were accompanied by attenuation of the characteristic coactive SIC, such that the resulting pattern could resemble parallel self-terminating processing.
Variability in drift direction, by contrast, produced little systematic relationship between accuracy and RT and largely preserved the coactive signature.

The LDLIV simulations extended this result to parallel self-terminating processing: slow errors generated by racing alone did not compromise its positive SIC, whereas added drift-rate variability differentiated the CAFs across conditions and progressively weakened that signature.

Collectively, these findings show that errors do not necessarily undermine architectural inference; the greater threat arises when their timing and prevalence differ across factorial conditions, causing correct-only analysis to reshape the contributing RT distributions unequally.
We next discuss the pCDM as a distinctive realization of coactive processing before considering the broader implications of error-related SIC attenuation.
The present simulations use the pCDM as a specific realization of coactive processing.

Generally, coactivation refers to architectures in which information from multiple sources is pooled before the decision is made (Townsend & Nozawa, 1995; Houpt & Townsend, 2011; Townsend & Houpt, 2025).
text.formatted: Generally, coactivation refers to architectures in which information from multiple sources is pooled before the decision is made <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Townsend & Nozawa, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Houpt & Townsend, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Townsend & Houpt, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The pCDM satisfies this functional definition because evidence from the two stimulus dimensions jointly determines the evolution and termination of a single diffusion process.
Unlike conventional coactive models, which mostly reduce evidence from multiple sources to a scalar sum, the pCDM retains the two-dimensional structure of the evidence throughout accumulation.

It therefore provides a useful case for examining whether established SIC predictions generalize to a form of coactivation in which the relative strength and variability of the component sources remain explicitly represented.
A distinctive feature of the pCDM, as a multidimensional stochastic decision process, is its relationship to General Recognition Theory (GRT; Ashby & Townsend, 1986).
text.formatted: A distinctive feature of the pCDM, as a multidimensional stochastic decision process, is its relationship to General Recognition Theory (GRT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ashby & Townsend, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: GRT represents multidimensional stimuli as probability distributions within a perceptual space and partitions that space using decision bounds.

The stochastic GRT model extends this framework to RT by allowing momentary perceptual representations to fluctuate over time and projecting them through a discriminant function onto a separate, unidimensional diffusion process (Ashby, 2000).

text.text: It therefore implements a two-stage form of coactivation: multidimensional perceptual information is first combined into a scalar discriminant value, which then drives evidence accumulation.
The pCDM provides a different stochastic extension of the same representational framework.

Rather than separating the stimulus representation from the accumulation process, it unifies them: evidence accumulates directly as a two-dimensional diffusion process within the stimulus-related evidence space and terminates at a circular absorbing boundary, defined in that same space.

Decision bounds partition the absorbing boundary into response regions, and the joint distributions of choice and RT are obtained from the locations and times at which trajectories first reach those regions.
This construction makes the effects of relationships between stimulus dimensions directly expressible in the model's predictions.

Differences in their relative evidence strength, variances, and covariance can influence both the direction in which the process travels and the time required to reach the boundary, thereby jointly determining response probabilities and RT distributions.
The pCDM consequently provides a natural framework for studying how multidimensional evidence interactions affect SFT diagnostics.
The same latent representation also supports different task instructions without requiring a different accumulation process.
In the present simulations, the AND and OR tasks were generated from the same partitioned evidence space and differed only in which boundaryhitting regions were grouped to define a correct response.
In the AND task, a correct affirmative response required termination in the region representing successful identification of both stimuli.
In the OR task, termination in any region representing identification of at least one stimulus was sufficient.

The OR-task correct-response distribution therefore contained a mixture of trajectories corresponding to accurate identification of both stimuli and trajectories corresponding to accurate identification of only one.
This mixture is ordinarily latent in behavioral data but can be identified directly within the pCDM through the boundary region in which each trajectory terminates.
We consider this common representation under different tasks as a modeling constraint rather than a claim that observers necessarily use identical representations under AND and OR instructions.

Nevertheless, holding the latent process constant provides a useful theoretical benchmark: it isolates the consequences of the stopping rule and response mapping from changes in the underlying representation.

Systematic empirical departures from this benchmark would be theoretically informative because they would suggest that task instructions alter how stimulus information is represented or accumulated, rather than merely how a common evidence state is categorized at response.
The decomposition of cross-trial drift-rate variability further illustrates the value of preserving the multidimensional evidence space.
Radial variability, 𝜂 )+, , changes the magnitude of the joint drift and therefore directly affects the effective rate of accumulation.
Tangential variability, 𝜂 -+. , changes the direction of the drift while leaving its overall magnitude comparatively stable.

It consequently alters the relative balance of evidence across stimulus dimensions and the proportions of trajectories terminating in different response regions but has much less influence on boundary-crossing time.

This form of variability has been theoretically associated with the division of a limited cognitive resource across stimulus representations, including sample-size model accounts of memory capacity (Lilburn et al., 2019; Lilburn & Smith, 2020; Sewell et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2025).

text.text: Across both AND and OR tasks, increasing 𝜂 -+. altered response accuracy and, particularly in the OR task, the mixture of latent outcomes contributing to correct responses.
Nevertheless, it produced little change in the relationship between accuracy and RT and largely preserved the characteristic coactive SIC.
By contrast, radial variability generated conditiondependent slow errors and progressively attenuated the SIC.
Because the processing architecture was held fixed by construction, this dissociation shows that representational variability does not inevitably compromise architectural diagnosis.
When variability changes the relative balance of evidence without systematically coupling accuracy to boundary-crossing time, the SIC continues to recover the unchanged coactive architecture.
This result is consistent with recent empirical application of SFT (Fong et al., 2024), which suggested that the processing architecture remains invariant with increasing stimulus set size.

text.text: Townsend and Nozawa (1995) defined coactivation as an architecture in which activation from two or more parallel channels is pooled into a common channel and compared with a single decision boundary.
For a coactive Poisson-counter model, they derived the canonical SIC signature as an early negative component followed by a larger positive component.

Unlike their distribution-general predictions for standard serial and parallel architectures, however, this coactive prediction was initially established only for a particular class of counting processes. Houpt and Townsend (2011) subsequently extended the result to coactive Wiener diffusion processes, showing that the canonical signature was not restricted to discrete-state Poisson accumulation.
text.formatted: Unlike their distribution-general predictions for standard serial and parallel architectures, however, this coactive prediction was initially established only for a particular class of counting processes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Houpt and Townsend (2011)</ref> subsequently extended the result to coactive Wiener diffusion processes, showing that the canonical signature was not restricted to discrete-state Poisson accumulation.

text.text: Together, these studies suggested that the SIC pattern might reflect a broader property of coactive evidence pooling, although its generality across different stochastic implementations remained uncertain.

Townsend and Houpt (2025) substantially expanded the analytic foundation of this prediction, proved that the canonical coactive SIC is generated by a coactive linear ballistic accumulator (Theorem 2.1), the broader class of inhomogeneous Poisson processes (Theorem 2.2), and the newly introduced bare-bones accrual model (Theorem 3.1).
They also derived sufficient conditions under which more general monotonic activation processes produce an early negative SIC followed by a larger positive component (Theorem 2.3).
These results considerably broaden the range of coactive models known to produce the canonical signature.
The pCDM implements coactivation through a different state-space structure.

In the models considered by Townsend and Houpt (2025), two independent, nondecreasing activation processes are collapsed into a scalar sum, 𝑋 7 (𝑡) + 𝑋 8 (𝑡), and only this pooled quantity is compared with a single boundary.
text.formatted: In the models considered by <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Townsend and Houpt (2025)</ref>, two independent, nondecreasing activation processes are collapsed into a scalar sum, 𝑋 7 (𝑡) + 𝑋 8 (𝑡), and only this pooled quantity is compared with a single boundary.

text.text: The pCDM instead preserves the two evidence components as coordinates of a common vector throughout accumulation.
Their joint magnitude determines when the circular boundary is reached, while their relative values determine where it is reached and, consequently, which response is produced.
Thus, evidence is combined without discarding its dimensional configuration.
Moreover, the component states can fluctuate in both directions, unlike the monotonic accrual assumed in Townsend and Houpt's general proof.

The pCDM therefore satisfies the functional principle that multiple evidence sources jointly drive a common decision process, but it is not a scalar summed-activation model and falls outside the class covered by their analytic results.

Despite these differences, the pCDM recovered the canonical coactive SIC in our baseline simulations, and this signature remained largely stable when variability altered the direction rather than the magnitude of the joint drift.

This provides constructive simulation evidence that the canonical pattern can extend beyond scalar summed-activation models to a multidimensional diffusion in which the magnitude and direction of evidence jointly determine RT and choice.

This conclusion is narrower than Townsend and Houpt (2025), as we demonstrate the result through simulation rather than proving it for the entire class of pCDMs or multidimensional diffusion processes.

text.text: Our simulations also identify an additional boundary condition.

When error prevalence and timing substantially differed across factorial conditions, conditioning on correct responses attenuated the canonical SIC even though the coactive architecture remained fixed.

Thus, the present findings both broaden and constrain the emerging generality of the coactive signature: a geometrically distinct coactive process can produce the predicted SIC, but the empirical recoverability of that signature depends on how response accuracy selects the distributions entering its calculation, as we now discuss in more details.
The central result of the present study is that excluding error responses can alter the SIC even when the underlying processing architecture remains unchanged.
This distortion does not arise merely because errors are present.
It arises when the probability and timing of errors differ across the HH, HL, LH, and LL conditions, causing the correct-response RT distributions to represent differently selected subsets of trials.
Because the SIC is computed from a contrast among these four distributions, condition-dependent selection need not cancel and may instead change the magnitude or shape of the resulting function.
The direction of this effect depends on where errors occur within the RT distributions.
Slow errors disproportionately remove observations from the later portions of the affected distributions.
When this selection is strongest in LL and weaker in the mixed and HH conditions, the retained correct-response distributions become more similar, progressively attenuating the SIC.
Fast errors instead remove observations from the leading edges of the correct-response distributions, again with the largest effect generally occurring in the lower-quality conditions.
This changes the early separation among the survivor functions and can alter the corresponding SIC components in a different direction.

Fast and slow errors therefore do not distort diagnosticity in the same way, they reshape different portions of the distributions entering the SIC and consequently produce distinct forms of distortion.

Historically, this issue may have had limited practical impact because DFP experiments have generally been applied to tasks that produce highly accurate performance (Houpt et al., 2014; Little et al., 2017).

text.text: Carefully calibrated stimulus setup and the general application of small-N design (Smith & Little, 2018; Little & Smith, 2018) in typical SFT tasks has limited the potential effect of error exclusion.

text.text: Likewise, our results here do not imply that conclusions from previous literature are invalid.

Nevertheless, our results identify a vulnerability that becomes increasingly relevant as SFT has recently trended to account for more difficult tasks, in which substantial error rates are theoretically informative.
Little et al. (2022) provided the first systematic extension of SFT to error responses by deriving SIC predictions separately for RT distributions conditioned on correct and incorrect responses.

Their analysis showed that canonical architectural signatures can be recovered from either response class, provided that the required ordering relations between factorial conditions are preserved and that exhaustive processing is necessary and sufficient for the relevant response.

Importantly, their model analysis demonstrated that these conditions hold for broad classes of Wiener diffusion models, including models with cross-trial parameter variability, but may fail for some Poisson-counter models.
Our results provide an important qualification to this conclusion.

Consistent with the diffusion-model proofs in Appendix A of Little et al. (2022), the expected ordering of the correct-response survivor functions was generally preserved under cross-trial parameter variability.
text.formatted: Consistent with the diffusion-model proofs in Appendix A of <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Little et al. (2022)</ref>, the expected ordering of the correct-response survivor functions was generally preserved under cross-trial parameter variability.

text.text: We extended this observation to a coactive architecture using the pCDM, which accumulates evidence jointly in a two-dimensional space and therefore complements the serial and parallel structures considered in their principal derivations.

However, our result further suggested that preserved stochastic ordering did not ensure that the diagnostic components of the SIC remained sufficiently pronounced to distinguish competing architectures.
This does not contradict Little et al.'s formal results, which concern the qualitative sign and shape of the population SIC under specified assumptions.
Instead, our result identifies a practical limitation: a theoretically consistent SIC component may become too small to detect reliably.
A closely related result appears in the parallel self-terminating OR simulation reported in Figure 10 of Little et al. (2022).
text.formatted: A closely related result appears in the parallel self-terminating OR simulation reported in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_15">10</ref> of <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Little et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Under Poisson Race Model I, when accuracy became low and strongly disproportionate across factorial conditions, the correct-response survivor functions converged despite retaining their ordering, and the SIC approached zero.

This convergence occurred alongside pronounced differences in accuracy across the factorial conditions: Their table 6 reports correct-response probabilities of .75, .57, .58, and .26 for HH, HL, LH, and LL, respectively.
Our racing-diffusion simulations reproduce the broader phenomenon using LDLIV as a different implementation of the same parallel self-terminating processing.
In our result, slow errors were present even without cross-trial drift-rate variability, but the SIC remained diagnostic while their effects were relatively balanced across conditions.
Attenuation emerged as increasing variability concentrated errors disproportionately in the lower-quality conditions.

Together, the two studies indicate that the presence of errors alone is not sufficient to compromise an SIC; the more consequential factor is how conditioning on accuracy differentially selects responses across the four factorial conditions. Gondan and Legner (2026) provide a complementary response to the limitations of accuracy-conditioned SICs.

However, this pooled distribution does not distinguish between correct and incorrect outcomes.

Unlike conditional RT distributions, these subdistributions are not normalized separately to one: their asymptotes equal the probabilities of correct and error responses.
They consequently preserve information about both when a response occurs and how frequently that response is produced.

This construction integrates RT and accuracy within a common nonparametric analysis, paralleling parametric analysis based on sequential sampling models.
The analysis proposed in Gondan and Legner (2026) is tightly related to the selection mechanism examined in the present study.

Dividing each retained subdistribution by its condition-specific accuracy then rescales it to a complete distribution, concealing how much probability mass was removed.

Our findings also relate to the architectural mimicry identified by Gondan and Legner's inference.

text.text: Consequently, although these contrasts jointly characterize how RT and accuracy interact across factorial conditions, none distinguishes parallel from serial self-terminating processing in this setting.
Gondan and Legner's framework therefore extends SFT to tasks with appreciable errors but does not guarantee unique architectural identification.
Instead, it reveals that incorporating response accuracy can introduce new model mimicries, requiring additional task conditions or theoretical constraints to distinguish the competing architectures.
This model mimicry is consistent with the broader conclusion of the present simulations.

In Gondan and Legner's derivations, the error contrast partially offsets the correct contrast, and the magnitude of this cancellation depends on the accumulation failures produced across factorial conditions.

In our simulations, the analogous imbalance is visible in the condition- The present results also suggest further constraints of empirical application of the DFP, such that controlling overall accuracy alone may not be sufficient.
Researchers should consider examining accuracy separately in the HH, HL, LH, and LL conditions, because a moderate aggregate error rate may conceal a pronounced concentration of errors in LL.
This examination is especially relevant, as the LL is usually the condition most susceptible to behavioral fluctuation.
Large discrepancies between LL and the remaining conditions should consequently be treated as a warning that the correct-response survivor functions may have been differentially selected.
This is not an argument for a universal accuracy cutoff, because the consequences of a given error rate depend on when the errors occur and how they are distributed across conditions.
Condition-specific accuracy and the temporal distribution of errors are more informative than overall accuracy alone.
The CAFs provide a useful companion to the SIC for this purpose.
Plotting the CAFs for the factorial conditions together reveals both whether accuracy changes systematically with RT and whether that relationship differs across four factorial conditions.
In addition to the condition-specific error rate, the empirical task instructions also require attention.
Strong emphasis on speed can increase early, noise-driven errors, whereas strong emphasis on accuracy can increase the prevalence of slow errors under weak or variable evidence.

Instructions should therefore be standardized carefully across participants and conditions, and pilot testing should aim to avoid extreme speed-accuracy regimes unless that trade-off is itself the object of study (Donkin et al., 2014).

text.text: Taken together, current results support a broader empirical workflow in which condition-specific error pattern, stochastic ordering, and SICs are evaluated jointly.

An SIC should be regarded as most secure when the required survivor ordering is preserved, error rates remain reasonably balanced across the factorial conditions, and the CAFs provide little evidence that correct-response selection differs systematically among those conditions.
When these criteria are not met, the observed SIC is still informative, but it should be treated with caution as a signature of the underlying architecture.
In conclusion, our study tested the validity of SIC-based architectural diagnoses under different error patterns across four conditions of the double-factorial design.

Across coactive and parallel self-terminating models, disproportionately removing slow or fast errors from the survivor functions systematically altered the SIC, despite the underlying processing architecture remaining unchanged.
These findings identify error-related selection as an important boundary condition for SFT.
Examining CAFs alongside SICs provides a direct, nonparametric means of detecting this risk and should strengthen the interpretation of SFT in tasks that produce appreciable errors.

Columns show increasing cross-trial drift-rate variability across the two stimulus specific CAFs: slow errors disproportionately remove later LL responses and attenuate the correct-response SIC, whereas fast errors remove earlier responses and alter it in a different direction.
CAFs therefore remain useful alongside unconditional contrasts because they reveal the temporal source of the response probabilities entering those contrasts.

Finally,Gondan and    Legner explicitly left coactive architectures for further derivations, whereas our pCDM simulations show that error-related selection can also compromise discrimination between coactive and parallel self-terminating signatures.

The present study thus complements their formal extension by clarifying the mechanisms underlying condition-dependent error distributions and by extending consideration of their consequences to a multidimensional coactive process.
